The Work, Thought and Legacy of Rabbi Eliyah Shapira (the "Eliyah Rabbah"): A Comprehensive Study in History, Halakha and Bibliography
Historical Background, Life Story and Spiritual Environment
Rabbi Eliyah Shapira (5420, c. 1660 – 8 Nisan 5472, 14 April 1712) stands as a central landmark in the halakhic and communal dynamics of Central European Jewry at the end of the seventeenth century and the beginning of the eighteenth [cite: 1, 2]. His figure grew out of the most distinguished rabbinic elite in the city of Prague, which was at that time a spiritual, scholarly and leadership center of the first rank in the Holy Roman Empire and in the entire Bohemian-Ashkenazi region [cite: 1, 2]. His father, Rabbi Binyamin Wolf Shapira, served as preacher and dayan in Prague, and in time was appointed Av Beit Din of the community and rabbi of the Land of Bohemia, positions that gave the family firm and influential leadership standing [cite: 2, 3].
Rabbi Eliyah's youth was marked by Torah mobility between the study centers of Bohemia and Poland [cite: 1, 2, 3]. To broaden his studies he traveled to the city of Kalisz, where he acquired Torah from the greatest scholars of his generation [cite: 1, 2, 3]. On his return to Prague he was integrated into the Torah and judicial leadership structure of the community [cite: 2, 3]. Around the year 5448 (1688) he was appointed rabbi of the city of Kolín in Bohemia, a position he held until around the year 5455 (1694) [cite: 2]. After this period he returned to Prague and was appointed a dayan in the community's chief court, known in the sources as "Moreh Shaveh" [cite: 2]. Around the year 5459 (1699) he received an approach from the community of Tiktin in Poland to serve as their rabbi, following the move of Rabbi Aryeh Leib Sirkis to Kraków [cite: 2]. In research and in the Torah literature there is a historical dispute over whether he accepted the invitation and actually served there for a short period before returning to Prague, or whether he preferred to decline the offer and remain in the study center of Prague [cite: 2]. In Prague he served, alongside his post as dayan, also as head of a yeshiva ("rosh metivta") and as the community's official preacher [cite: 2, 3].
The family environment of Rabbi Eliyah Shapira reflected the network of Torah and social ties of the leadership of his generation [cite: 2, 3]. His brother-in-law, his father's son-in-law, was the Gaon Rabbi Yaakov Reischer, author of the halakhic and responsa literature "Chok Yaakov," "Shevut Yaakov" and "Minchat Yaakov" [cite: 3]. His wife, Dabrish (who died in 5485), was the daughter of R. Azriel Yom Tov Bondi, one of the parnasim of Prague [cite: 2]. His children continued the dynasty of rabbis and public service [cite: 2]: his son Rabbi Aryeh Leib served as Av Beit Din of Leipnik and died in his father's lifetime in the year 5472 [cite: 2]; his son Rabbi Shmuel later served as Av Beit Din of Prague [cite: 2]; his son R. Shimon was one of the parnasim of Prague Jewry and married the daughter of R. Binyamin Wolf, son of Rabbi Aharon Shimon Shapira [cite: 2]; and his daughter Rivka married R. Wolf Segal Frankel, son of Rabbi Yissachar Berman Segal Frankel, author of "Matteh Yissachar" [cite: 2]. Rabbi Eliyah Shapira died in the prime of his years, in his father's lifetime, at only about 52, on 8 Nisan 5472 (1712), and was buried in the ancient Jewish cemetery in Prague [cite: 2, 3].

His Teachers and Spiritual Influences
The Torah and halakhic teaching of Rabbi Eliyah Shapira was shaped from a fusion of two central traditions of study of that period: the Polish halakhic-scholastic tradition on the one hand, and the Ashkenazi-Bohemian tradition of the beit midrash and of custom on the other [cite: 1, 2, 3, 4]. This fusion derived directly from the personality and authority of his distinguished teachers [cite: 1, 2, 3].
His grandfather, his father's father, Rabbi Aharon Shimon Shapira (known in halakhic literature as the Maharash of Prague), served as mara de-atra, Av Beit Din and head of the yeshiva in Prague, and was regarded as the distinguished teacher of Rabbi Eliyah [cite: 1, 2, 3]. Rabbi Eliyah frequently cites him in his works by the reverent epithet "my grandfather the Gaon," and from him he adopted a meticulous loyalty to the ancient customs of Prague and to rooted Ashkenazi halakhic ruling [cite: 2, 3, 4].
On the other hand, his period of study in Kalisz with Rabbi Avraham Abele HaLevi Gombiner, author of the "Magen Avraham," shaped his analytical and corpus-based approach [cite: 1, 2, 3]. From the Magen Avraham he acquired the aspiration to investigate the sources of the law down to their foundations in the Talmud and in the words of the Rishonim, the demand to be precise in the language of the poskim, and the willingness to confront earlier poskim [cite: 1, 2, 5, 6]. Alongside these, he also studied in Prague with Rabbi Shmuel Helman, one of the city's important dayanim, who instilled in him the method of legal discussion practiced in the community's courts [cite: 2].
His Books and Works: The Philosophy of Interpretation for a Torah Enterprise
The literary enterprise of Rabbi Eliyah Shapira comprises halakhic works, Talmudic novellae and homiletic books [cite: 2, 3, 7]. The work "Eliyah Zuta" is a concise and condensed commentary that gathers the main laws and comments on the books of the "Levush" by Rabbi Mordechai Yaffe ("Levush HaTekhelet" and "Levush HaChur," which parallel the Orach Chaim section of the Shulchan Arukh) [cite: 1, 2]. This book was printed in the author's lifetime in two editions in Prague (in 5449/1689 and in 5461/1701), and since then its printing has been fixed as an inseparable part of the editions of the book "Levush" [cite: 2].
His central and most influential work, "Eliyah Rabbah," was written originally as a broad, comprehensive and in-depth commentary on the books of the "Levush" [cite: 2, 3]. The work presents a detailed halakhic discussion, including extensive give-and-take in the words of the Rishonim and Acharonim, clarification of textual versions and decision of the halakha in practice [cite: 8]. The history of its printing was full of historical upheavals [cite: 2, 3, 8, 9]: the work was not printed in the author's lifetime, and after his death his family members and students labored to bring it to print from copies [cite: 2, 3]. The author's original, autograph manuscript was burned entirely in the great fire that consumed the Jewish quarter of Prague in the year 5514 (1754), together with other manuscripts of the author [cite: 3, 8, 9]. The work was saved only thanks to a copy made in good time, which, according to the testimony of the publishers, was in part deficient and blurred [cite: 3]. When the work was brought to print, the editors made a typographical decision to print the "Eliyah Rabbah" as a book arranged on the order of the "Shulchan Arukh" and not around the book "Levush" [cite: 2, 3]. This decision often caused misunderstanding among learners, since the precisions and objections of the "Eliyah Rabbah" were originally directed at the language of the "Levush" and not at the wording of Maran the Shulchan Arukh [cite: 2, 3]. In modern editions the work was restored to its original form and is printed alongside the books of the "Levush" or as an independent book with its own original opening words (dibburim hamatchilim) [cite: 2, 3].
Besides his halakhic works, Rabbi Eliyah Shapira composed a book of novellae and commentaries on tractates of the Babylonian Talmud, which is also called "Eliyah Rabbah," and which was first printed by his grandson in Fürth in the year 5528 (1768) [cite: 2, 3, 7]. By virtue of his position as the community's preacher in Prague he also composed a book of homilies on the Torah, and he also left behind responsa in halakha, but these manuscripts went up in flames in the Prague fire of the year 5514 and most of them were not privileged to see the light [cite: 2, 3, 8, 9].
Title of the work | Subject and genre | Format and printing | Status and fate of the work
Eliyah Zuta | A short commentary on the Levush (Orach Chaim) | Printed in his lifetime (Prague 5449, 5461) [cite: 2] | Printed regularly in all the editions of the "Levush" [cite: 2]
Eliyah Rabbah (on the Levush) | A broad commentary and halakhic ruling (Orach Chaim) | Printed after his death from a manuscript copy [cite: 2, 3] | The original was burned in 5514; mistakenly adapted to the Shulchan Arukh and from there into an independent book [cite: 2, 3, 8, 9]
Eliyah Rabbah (on the Shas) | Novellae on tractates of the Talmud | Printed in Fürth 5528 (1768) [cite: 2, 3, 7] | Printed by his grandson from manuscripts that survived [cite: 2, 3, 7]
Book of homilies and responsa | Homilies on the Torah and responsa | In manuscript | Lost almost entirely in the Prague fire of the year 5514 [cite: 3, 8, 9]
His Halakhic Method, His Way of Study and Bibliographic Precision
The halakhic method of the author of the "Eliyah Rabbah" is characterized by a combination of deep analytical scholarship together with an inclination toward practical and clear decision [cite: 8]. Intellectual independence is evident in his halakhic discussions: on the one hand, the work was written around the text of the "Levush" out of great appreciation for the codification enterprise of Rabbi Mordechai Yaffe [cite: 2]. On the other hand, the "Eliyah Rabbah" does not shrink from objecting to the "Levush" when he finds that the latter deviated from the ancient custom of Ashkenaz or from the decision of the Gemara and the Rishonim [cite: 4, 5, 10]. Rabbi Eliyah displays a similar attitude toward his distinguished teacher, the author of the "Magen Avraham" [cite: 1, 2, 5, 11]. In many cases he confronts the novellae of the Magen Avraham with references in the Rishonim or with the custom of Prague, and rules contrary to the words of his teacher [cite: 5, 11, 12, 13].
One of the prominent hallmarks of the book "Eliyah Rabbah" is its exceptional bibliographic richness [cite: 8]. The Chida, in his book "Machazik Berakha," lavishly praised it and wrote that the "Eliyah Rabbah" searched in all the chambers of the libraries of the righteous, and all the books of devei rav are surveyed before him [cite: 8], and likewise the author of the "Chayei Adam" wrote in his introduction that the book is highly esteemed because the author had before him all the books of the Rishonim and also many manuscripts [cite: 8]. Nevertheless, over the years editors and learners came out against what appeared to be many citation errors and mistaken references in the book, as the author of the "Chayei Adam" remarked in his time that the book contains many scribal errors [cite: 8].
A thorough bibliographic study printed in recent years proved that the notion of the "many printing errors" in the "Eliyah Rabbah" was fundamentally mistaken and stemmed from the bibliographic ignorance of modern editors regarding the exact editions and manuscripts that lay on the desk of Rabbi Eliyah Shapira at the end of the seventeenth century [cite: 8]. Rabbi Eliyah Shapira used rare first printed editions that differ in their structure, in the numbering of their sections and in the division of their pages from the editions common today [cite: 8]:
The citations of Sefer Chasidim in the "Eliyah Rabbah," which appear more than 180 times, correspond exactly to the first printing (Bologna 5298), in which the numbering of the sections is entirely different from the later printings [cite: 8]. His references to the book Shibbolei HaLeket, brought more than 250 times, correspond to the first, abridged edition (Venice 5306), which was the only printing available in his time, and not to the edition of the "complete Shibbolei HaLeket" that was printed from manuscripts hundreds of years later [cite: 8]. Similarly, the citations of Sefer Yere'im correspond to the abridgment of Sefer Yere'im (Venice edition 5326), which was common in his time, and not to the complete edition that was printed only at the end of the nineteenth century [cite: 8]. Likewise, the quotations from the responsa of the Maharil correspond to the Hanau edition (5370), in which the numbering of the sections was changed and errors were corrected according to manuscripts, and not to the Cremona printings [cite: 8]. Even the references to the book "Ma'adanei Melech," which many editors hastened to "correct" to "Ma'adanei Yom Tov," are faithful to the original name of the work before its name was changed by the author [cite: 8].
The book cited in the "Eliyah Rabbah" | The edition the author had before him | The gap from the editions common today | Significance of the bibliographic discovery
Sefer Chasidim | First printing, Bologna 5298 (1538) [cite: 8] | Section numbering completely different from the Margaliot printings [cite: 8] | The section references are entirely accurate according to the Bologna printing [cite: 8]
Shibbolei HaLeket | Venice printing 5306 (1546) [cite: 8] | The abridgment of Shibbolei HaLeket (the only one printed in his time) [cite: 8] | The reference to pages and sections corresponds exactly to this edition [cite: 8]
Sefer Yere'im | Abridgment of Yere'im, Venice printing 5326 (1566) [cite: 8] | The "complete Yere'im" was printed only at the end of the nineteenth century [cite: 8] | The references correspond to the abridgment that was common in the seventeenth century [cite: 8]
Responsa of the Maharil | Hanau edition 5370 (1610) [cite: 8] | Section numbering different from the Cremona printing of 5316 [cite: 8] | The references correspond to the corrected Hanau edition [cite: 8]
Ma'adanei Yom Tov | An earlier edition under the name "Ma'adanei Melech" [cite: 8] | The later change of name by the author [cite: 8] | The original reference of the author of the "Eliyah Rabbah" was accurate for its time [cite: 8]
His Students, His Influence and His Legacy for Generations
The students of Rabbi Eliyah Shapira in Prague carried the torch of his Torah after his death in his prime, labored to copy his manuscripts, and brought his work "Eliyah Rabbah" to the printing press [cite: 2, 3]. His books, and above all the book "Eliyah Rabbah," were received in the world of Torah and halakha with exceptional favor and became an iron possession of Ashkenazi halakhic ruling [cite: 2, 3, 8].
The central poskim of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries saw the author of the "Eliyah Rabbah" as a decisive halakhic authority. The Chida, in his books "Machazik Berakha" and "Shem HaGedolim," treated his method with great respect, noting his comprehensive mastery [cite: 8]; the author of the "Chayei Adam" based many discussions on him in the Orach Chaim section and regarded him as one of the fathers of halakhic instruction [cite: 8]; and eminent poskim such as the author of the "Shulchan Arukh HaRav," the author of the "Arukh HaShulchan" and the author of the "Kitzur Shulchan Arukh" frequently cited his decisions as a basis for the accepted ruling in the communities of Ashkenaz and Poland [cite: 14, 15, 16, 17, 18].
The peak of the influence of the "Eliyah Rabbah" can be seen in the book "Mishnah Berurah" by Maran Rabbi Yisrael Meir HaKohen of Radin [cite: 2, 3, 12, 14, 19]. The "Mishnah Berurah" sees in the "Eliyah Rabbah" one of the four central pillars of halakhic instruction of the Orach Chaim section among the Acharonim, alongside the Magen Avraham, the Taz and the Dagul MeRevava [cite: 2, 3, 12, 14, 15]. In thousands of places throughout the work the "Mishnah Berurah" brings the decision of the "Eliyah Rabbah," and at frequent times, when there is a dispute between the Taz and the Magen Avraham, the "Mishnah Berurah" chooses to decide in accordance with the position of the "Eliyah Rabbah," which served him as a mediating and deciding factor in the Ashkenazi beit midrash [cite: 2, 3, 12, 13, 14, 15].
Summary and Conclusions
Rabbi Eliyah Shapira of Prague, author of the "Eliyah Rabbah," stands in the front rank of the Ashkenazi poskim at the transition from the seventeenth century to the eighteenth [cite: 1, 2]. His Torah leadership, which extended across Prague, Kolín and the expanses of Bohemia and Poland, uniquely fused the beit midrash study tradition of Prague with the broad halakhic analysis of the Torah centers of Poland [cite: 1, 2, 3, 4].
His written enterprise, despite the heavy disaster of the burning of his manuscripts in the year 5514, left an indelible mark on the world of halakha [cite: 3, 8, 9]. His book "Eliyah Rabbah," written originally as a commentary on the "Levush," became, thanks to its depth, its mastery and its bibliographic comprehensiveness, a foundational book in the ruling of halakha in Orach Chaim [cite: 2, 3, 8]. Modern bibliographic research completed the picture of the figure, proving that what had been regarded across generations as a "printing error" in his work is nothing but testimony to his meticulousness and to his use of rare printed editions and manuscripts that lay before him [cite: 8]. His central standing in the halakhic books of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, and the first place he holds in the book "Mishnah Berurah," secure the place of the author of the "Eliyah Rabbah" as one of the fathers of Ashkenazi halakhic ruling throughout the generations [cite: 2, 3, 12, 14, 15, 19].
